name: US Politics News
tagline: Midterms, Congress and the White House — explained daily.

articles.title: Jeffries Launches Speaker Bid With Affordability Agenda After Democrats Win Congress
articles.description: Hakeem Jeffries formally launched his bid to become the first Black Speaker of the House, outlining a first-100-days agenda on affordability, oversight and tariffs after Democrats won both chambers.
articles.sources: ABC News via DD India, Mathrubhumi, Free Malaysia Today, EconoTimes, November 5, 2026
articles.body:
House Democratic Leader Hakeem Jeffries formally launched his bid to become the next Speaker of the House of Representatives on Wednesday, November 4, a day after Democrats won control of Congress in the midterm elections, ABC News reported. If elected when the new Congress convenes on January 3, 2027, the New York Democrat would become the first Black Speaker in American history.

A letter to colleagues

Jeffries announced his candidacy in a letter to Democratic colleagues, writing: “I write to humbly request your support in connection with my candidacy to serve as the next Speaker of the House of Representatives.” He closed by seeking backing “to serve as the 57th Speaker of the United States House of Representatives.” Democratic leadership elections are scheduled behind closed doors on November 18, reports said. Jeffries would need a simple majority of House Democrats to secure the party’s nomination, and then 218 votes on the House floor in January.

The affordability agenda

Jeffries outlined three priorities for the incoming Congress: affordability, accountability and American values. “In the new Congress, we will aggressively fight for an affordable America. Life is way too expensive, and millions of hardworking taxpayers are drowning in this failed economy,” he wrote. His first-100-days proposals include reversing Medicaid cuts, restoring SNAP food-assistance funding, extending Affordable Care Act tax credits, eradicating the Trump tariffs and stopping what he called the reckless war of choice in Iran, which he blamed for rising gasoline prices. Senate Democratic Leader Chuck Schumer welcomed the results, saying “Relief is on the way,” while also highlighting affordability and efforts to end the war in Iran.

Oversight and the road ahead

On accountability, Jeffries promised stronger congressional oversight of the Trump administration, measures against corruption and price gouging, and a ban on stock trading by members of Congress. “The days of the House functioning like a wholly owned subsidiary of the Trump Administration are over. Congress will assume its place as a check and balance on an out-of-control executive branch,” he wrote. He also said House Democrats had refused to fund what he called a violent mass-deportation machine, arguing immigration enforcement should be fair, just and humane. Late on Wednesday, Jeffries posted on X that House Democrats were on track to win at least 255 seats, according to reports. Any bill to roll back tariffs would still need to clear the Senate and face President Trump’s veto, so the agenda is a statement of intent, not enacted law. Outgoing Speaker Mike Johnson told staff he would not run for minority leader in the new Congress, reports said.

articles.title: Two Senate Races Still Uncalled: Alaska and Mississippi Counts Drag On After Democrats Secure Majority
articles.description: Democrats have already secured at least 54 Senate seats, but Alaska and Mississippi remain uncalled, with Democrats leading narrowly in both — Alaska's ranked-choice count is due November 18 and Mississippi counties must certify by November 13.
articles.sources: Associated Press, Firstpost, CBS News via Kacee Allen, Reuters, November 5, 2026
articles.body:
Democrats have secured a Senate majority in the 2026 midterms, but two races remain uncalled on November 5, with Democrats leading narrowly in both Alaska and Mississippi, according to the Associated Press and reports from CBS News and Reuters. Neither result would change which party controls the chamber — Democrats already hold at least 54 of the 100 seats — but the outcomes will decide the size of the incoming majority when the 120th Congress assembles on January 3, 2027.

Mississippi: a lead of about 1,100 votes

In Mississippi, Democrat Scott Colom leads Republican incumbent Senator Cindy Hyde-Smith by a wafer-thin margin, with about 96 percent of the vote counted, the Associated Press reported. Colom had secured 464,926 votes, or 49 percent, against Hyde-Smith’s 463,788 votes, or 48.9 percent — a lead of 1,138 votes. Decision Desk HQ’s later update put the gap at 1,852 votes. Around 3,600 outstanding mail-in ballots remain, along with an unknown number of provisional, or affidavit, ballots. Affidavit voters have until November 10 to submit identification, and counties have until November 13 to send certified results to the state.

Alaska: ranked choice means a long wait

In Alaska, Democrat Mary Peltola holds a narrow lead of 637 first-choice votes over Republican incumbent Senator Dan Sullivan — 102,962 to 102,325 — with about a quarter of votes still untallied, according to AP figures cited in reports. The race may take more than a week to call because Alaska uses ranked-choice voting: if no candidate wins more than 50 percent of first-choice votes, officials redistribute votes and announce the ranked-choice result on November 18, fifteen days after the polls, Alaska’s Division of Elections said. The contest was complicated by a same-name candidate, retired schoolteacher Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., whose presence federal prosecutors have been investigating, reports said.

The wider picture

Democrats flipped seven Republican-held Senate seats in the cycle — in Texas, Kansas, South Carolina, Maine, Iowa, Ohio and North Carolina — according to Fox News race calls cited in coverage, while holding all of their own seats. CBS News estimated Democrats would finish with between 251 and 268 House seats. With the House and Senate both set to be organised by Democrats in January, the remaining counts in Alaska and Mississippi are about margins, not control — but in a chamber where every vote matters for legislation and confirmations, the difference between 54 and 56 seats is still significant. Votes are still being counted in many states, so the figures above will change.

articles.title: Democrats Win Control of House and Senate in 2026 Midterms, AP Projects
articles.description: Democrats have won control of both chambers of Congress in the 2026 midterms, AP projected, flipping seven Senate seats and passing 218 in the House — though dozens of races were still uncalled on November 4.
articles.sources: Associated Press via Indian Express, CNN, Al Jazeera, Cointelegraph, November 4, 2026
articles.body:
Democrats have won control of both the House of Representatives and the Senate in the 2026 midterm elections, according to Associated Press projections reported on November 4, delivering a major setback to President Donald Trump and the Republicans in the final two years of his second term.

The tallies so far

Reports on November 4 put Democrats at 228 House seats to 139 for Republicans, past the 218 needed for a majority, with 68 House races still uncalled, and at 54 Senate seats to 44, with Alaska and Mississippi still being counted. Democrats flipped seven Republican-held Senate seats, according to ABC News and Fox News projections cited in coverage: Iowa, Kansas, Maine, North Carolina, Ohio, South Carolina and Texas. The party also held all of its own Senate seats, including Michigan, where Abdul El-Sayed won, and Minnesota, where Peggy Flanagan held on.

What changes — and what does not

Democratic control of Congress means the party sets the agenda in both chambers and gains broad oversight powers, but it does not on its own deliver legislation: the Senate filibuster remains, and President Trump can veto bills that reach his desk. Trump told Fox News, “Congratulations to the Democrats. They did a good job,” and told the Wall Street Journal he expected to work with them. The new Congress takes office on January 3, 2027, and Rep. Hakeem Jeffries is in line to become Speaker, reports said.

articles.title: Texas Breaks: Talarico Wins Senate, Hinojosa Ousts Abbott in First Democratic Statewide Sweep Since 1994
articles.description: Democrat James Talarico won the Texas Senate race and Gina Hinojosa defeated three-term Governor Greg Abbott, giving Democrats their first statewide wins in Texas since 1994, reports said on November 4.
articles.sources: CNN, Indian Express, Al Jazeera, November 4, 2026
articles.body:
Texas, long the emblem of Republican dominance, broke for Democrats on Tuesday: James Talarico won the open Senate race and Gina Hinojosa defeated three-term Republican Governor Greg Abbott, the first Democratic statewide victories in Texas since 1994, CNN and the Indian Express reported on November 4.

The Senate race

Talarico, a Democratic state legislator, defeated Republican Attorney General Ken Paxton, who had been endorsed by President Trump, in what became the most expensive Senate race in US history, CNN reported. It was the first Democratic Senate win in Texas since 1988. In Maine, Democrat Troy Jackson ousted five-term Republican Senator Susan Collins by almost seven points, and in Kansas, Democrat Adam Hamilton defeated Senator Roger Marshall — the party's first Kansas Senate win since 1932.

The governor's race — and the wider map

Hinojosa's defeat of Abbott was the night's other Texas shock, and she had campaigned in part on a moratorium on new data centres, a pledge markets noticed on Wednesday. Elsewhere, Democrat Amy Acton won the Ohio governorship, and in Georgia, Keisha Lance Bottoms became the first Black woman elected governor in US history and Georgia's first Democratic governor since 1998, reports said. Democrats also toppled Republican state legislative supermajorities in states including Indiana and Missouri, and won House races in districts Trump had carried by 20 points two years earlier.

articles.title: Election Day: Polls Open Across America After a Record 58 Million Early Votes
articles.description: Polls opened on Tuesday, November 3, for the 2026 midterm elections, with more than 58 million ballots already cast early — a midterm record — and no results reported yet.
articles.sources: LiveNewsWorld, Financial Express, Al Jazeera, November 3, 2026
articles.body:
Americans are voting on Tuesday, November 3, in midterm elections that will decide control of Congress for the final two years of President Donald Trump's second term, with polls opening across all 50 states and no results reported yet, live coverage reported.

A record early vote

More than 58 million people had cast ballots before Election Day, according to the University of Florida Election Lab, cited by CBS News and the Financial Express — a record for a midterm election, up from the 54 million reported on November 2. All 435 House seats, 35 Senate seats and 36 governorships are on the ballot. Republicans currently hold a 53-47 Senate advantage and a narrow House majority, so a handful of competitive races in states including Michigan, Ohio, North Carolina, Georgia and Iowa are expected to decide control.

Polls, monitors and the count ahead

Polls opened as early as 5 a.m. ET in Vermont and at 6 a.m. ET in states including Connecticut, Maine, New Jersey, New York and Virginia. The Justice Department said it would send roughly 1,000 election monitors across all 50 states, describing it as the largest federal monitoring effort in its history. The first polls close at 6 p.m. ET, and close races may take days to call as mail-in and provisional ballots are counted.

articles.title: Election Night: Forecasts Point One Way, but Control May Take Days to Call
articles.description: Forecasts agree Democrats are favoured to take the House, with the Senate closer — but with first polls closing at 6 p.m. ET, control could remain uncertain for days, reports said on November 3.
articles.sources: Asia Today, Al Jazeera, November 3, 2026
articles.body:
Forecasts published before Election Day point in the same direction but differ on confidence, and none of them is a result: voters, not models, decide control of Congress, reports on November 3 stressed.

What the models say

Decision Desk HQ's model, updated on October 29, gave Democrats an 80 percent chance in the House, with 238 seats projected, and a 60 percent chance in the Senate, with 52 seats projected. The Cook Political Report projected Democratic gains of 12 to 22 House seats and two to six Senate seats, while prediction markets priced Democratic control higher, at 92 to 93 percent for the House and 68 percent for the Senate. RealClearPolling put Democrats 8.3 points ahead on the generic congressional ballot, and a Reuters/Ipsos poll put President Trump's approval at 32 percent, near a record low.

Why the wait

Results start after the first polls close at 6 p.m. ET, but close races can take days, and final tallies can take days or weeks as mail-in and provisional ballots are counted. In Georgia, a Senate race with no majority winner goes to a run-off on December 1. Ranked-choice counts in states such as Alaska and Maine could also leave control uncertain, and the new Congress will take office on January 3, 2027. Early leads can shift as later ballots are counted, which on its own is not a sign of fraud, Al Jazeera noted.

articles.title: Trump's Closing Midterm Pitch From the Lincoln Memorial: 'I'll Become Mr Veto'
articles.description: President Donald Trump will deliver his final midterm pitch Monday from the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool, telling the New York Post he would veto Democratic bills if Republicans lose Congress — 'I'll become Mr Veto.'
articles.sources: Associated Press via The Week, ET Now, Times Now, November 2, 2026
articles.body:
President Donald Trump will make his final pitch to voters on Monday from the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool in Washington, a day before midterm elections that will decide control of Congress, according to White House announcements reported on November 2.

A Washington closing argument

The address is set for 2 p.m. ET and is described by the White House as Trump's closing message before the midterms. Rather than travelling to a battleground state on the final day, Trump chose the Reflecting Pool — a site tied to his controversial, problem-plagued renovation effort, which he said in April would take days and cost about $1.5 million but finished nearly three months behind schedule at more than ten times that estimate, the Associated Press reported. Trump told reporters his Sunday evening rally in Kansas, after a stop in Iowa, was 'my last stop' on the rally trail.

'I'll become Mr Veto'

In an interview with the New York Post's Miranda Devine, Trump laid out his plan if Democrats win Congress: 'I guess I'll become Mr Veto. I'm not going to let them ruin it,' adding, 'If we didn't win, I'd veto everything. I'll be vetoing, vetoing.' A veto rejects a bill passed by Congress, which can only be overridden by two-thirds of both chambers. Trump has used the power only twice in his second term, against ten vetoes in his first. All 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats are on the ballot on Tuesday, November 3.

articles.title: Final Polls Point to Democratic Gains as Record 54 Million Vote Early
articles.description: The final New York Times/Siena poll shows Democratic candidates leading in all seven most competitive seats, while early voting has already passed a midterm-record 54 million ballots, reports said on November 2.
articles.sources: Agence France-Presse via Philstar, The Source, November 2, 2026
articles.body:
Democrats enter Election Day with polls pointing to at least partial control of Congress, as a record early vote and a string of final surveys shape expectations for Tuesday, November 3, Agence France-Presse reported on November 2.

A record early vote

More than 54 million people have already cast ballots, a midterm record, up from the 51 million reported days earlier. Democrats held final get-out-the-vote rallies on Monday, including star Senate candidates James Talarico in Texas and Adam Hamilton in Kansas. Polls show Democrats near certain to take the House majority and with a real shot at the Senate, which Republicans currently hold 53-47.

What the final surveys say

The final New York Times/Siena poll released Sunday evening showed Democratic candidates leading in all seven seats viewed as most competitive, though five remained within the margin of error. An NBC News poll released Sunday showed 60 percent disapproving of the president's performance, particularly over high prices exacerbated by his eight-month war against Iran. In a sign of Democratic infighting, Michigan congresswoman Haley Stevens endorsed Republican Mike Rogers against progressive candidate Abdul El-Sayed in her state's key Senate race on Sunday. Polls are snapshots, not results — voters decide on Tuesday.

articles.title: FBI Alaska Probe and California Ballot Fight Intensify in Final Midterm Weekend
articles.description: Federal prosecutors are investigating an alleged candidate-recruitment effort in Alaska's Senate race while the Justice Department weighs a Supreme Court appeal over more than 20,000 California mail-in ballots, Reuters reported on November 1.
articles.sources: Reuters via TBS News, Outlook India, November 1, 2026
articles.body:
The Trump administration stepped up its legal and investigative efforts on the final weekend of the midterm campaign, as federal prosecutors investigated an alleged candidate-recruitment effort in Alaska's pivotal Senate race and the Justice Department said it would likely take its fight over thousands of California mail-in ballots to the Supreme Court, Reuters reported on November 1.

An Alaska investigation with Senate control at stake

In Alaska, federal prosecutors are investigating whether aides to Democratic challenger Mary Peltola helped recruit a retired schoolteacher, Daniel J. Sullivan Jr., to run because his name is similar to that of the Republican incumbent, Senator Dan S. Sullivan. The closely contested race is seen as crucial to Democrats' hopes of taking the Senate in Tuesday's vote. Alaska's Senate race is one of seven key toss-ups that will likely decide whether Republicans keep their 53-47 majority in the chamber.

California ballots head toward the Supreme Court

In California, a federal appeals court ruled 2-1 this week that the Justice Department had failed to justify its emergency bid to force the state to set aside postal ballots from more than 20,000 registered voters it alleges are likely to be non-citizens. Acting Deputy Attorney General Trent McCotter indicated on Saturday that the administration could take the dispute to the country's highest court. California Governor Gavin Newsom warned the state's top federal judges on Saturday that the Justice Department may seek warrants to seize ballots before results are certified, though he said he did not know of any pending request. Separately, the administration has sued roughly 30 states and the District of Columbia seeking unredacted voter rolls.

articles.title: Democrats Lead Generic Ballot by 8.2 Points as Early Voting Passes 51 Million
articles.description: Democrats lead Republicans 51.4% to 43.2% on the national congressional ballot, according to RealClearPolling's latest average, while more than 51 million Americans have already voted — a midterm record.
articles.sources: Al Jazeera, RealClearPolling, Economist/YouGov, November 1, 2026
articles.body:
With three days to go before the midterm elections, Democrats are leading national polls as millions of Americans cast their ballots early, Al Jazeera reported on November 1.

A record early vote

More than 51 million Americans have already cast ballots in person or by post, according to the University of Florida's Election Lab, up from nearly 46 million who voted before Election Day at the last midterms in 2022. The early-vote surge has drawn particular attention in Iowa and Kansas, where competitive Senate races are under way: Iowa had recorded more than 430,000 early ballots by Saturday morning, with registered Democrats accounting for more than 46% against 34% for Republicans, while Kansas had recorded more than 420,000 ballots, according to the Associated Press.

What the final polls say

According to RealClearPolling's latest national congressional ballot average, Democrats lead Republicans by 8.2 percentage points, 51.4% to 43.2%. A separate Economist/YouGov survey released on Thursday found that 44% of registered voters expect Democrats to control the House after the election, compared with 31% who expect Republicans to retain control. Polls are snapshots, not results: voters will decide all 435 House seats and 35 Senate seats on Tuesday, November 3, and close races can take days to call. President Trump is scheduled to close his campaign with rallies in Iowa and Kansas on Sunday, while Democrats make their final appeals in states including Texas, Michigan and Alaska.

articles.title: Early Voting Surges Past 47.9 Million as Texas Turnout Jumps 50% Ahead of the Midterms
articles.description: Nearly 47.9 million Americans had already voted before Election Day, according to the University of Florida's Election Lab, with early turnout running about 10 million ahead of the same point in 2022.
articles.sources: Associated Press via Times Now, University of Florida Election Lab, Indian Express, October 31, 2026
articles.body:
Early voting in the 2026 midterm elections has surged well past the pace of four years ago, with nearly 47.9 million ballots already cast before Election Day on Tuesday, November 3, according to data from the University of Florida's Election Lab reported on October 31.

A record early-vote pace

An Associated Press analysis of voting data covering 47 states and Washington, DC found nearly 10 million more early ballots cast than at the same point in 2022. The Election Lab put the national total at 47,922,669 early votes by midday on October 30, already ahead of the previous midterm early-voting record of about 45.9 million ballots cast in 2022.

The increase has been sharpest in states with competitive Senate races. In Texas, more than 6.3 million people had voted by Wednesday, compared with 4.2 million at the same point in 2022, a rise of about 50%. Early voting also rose by more than 30% in Maine, Michigan, North Carolina and Kansas, all home to competitive Senate contests. In states that report party affiliation, about 6.8 million Democrats and 5.2 million Republicans had cast early ballots, though those figures do not cover all early voters and do not show which candidates any voter supported.

What is at stake on Tuesday

Voters will decide all 435 House seats, 35 Senate seats and 36 governorships. Republicans currently hold a 53-47 majority in the Senate and a 218-214 edge in the House, and forecasters see a Democratic House as likely while the Senate remains close, with control resting on a handful of toss-up races. Early-vote totals are a measure of turnout, not a result: states certify outcomes only after completing their canvass, and close races can take days to call.

articles.title: Trump Rallies in Daytona Beach, Then Heads to Iowa and Kansas on Sunday After Canceled Stops
articles.description: President Trump spoke at a rally in Daytona Beach, Florida, on Friday night and will now hold rallies in Kansas and Iowa on Sunday, November 1, a day after those stops were canceled.
articles.sources: Indian Express live election coverage, New York Times, October 31, 2026
articles.body:
President Donald Trump addressed supporters at a rally at the Ocean Center in Daytona Beach, Florida, on Friday night, in the final weekend of campaigning before Tuesday's midterm elections, according to live election coverage on October 31.

Iowa and Kansas back on the schedule

Trump will now hold rallies in Kansas and Iowa on Sunday, November 1, a day after those stops were canceled in favor of tele-rallies, the coverage reported. The reversal restores in-person events in two states with unexpectedly competitive Senate races, after the president had instead planned to campaign virtually across nearly 20 states. Former Vice President Kamala Harris campaigned for Democrats in Atlanta on Friday, as both parties made their final case to voters in the races that will decide control of Congress.

Courts and ballot fights continue

A federal appeals court on Friday again refused to order California to set aside more than 20,000 mail-in ballots, rejecting an administration effort that a court described as unconstitutional, according to the same coverage. The Justice Department has also widened its subpoenas in California and Alaska, the New York Times reported, as election officials brace for further legal challenges in the final days before polls close.

articles.title: Trump Cancels Iowa and Kansas Rallies, Switching to Tele-Rallies Across Nearly 20 States
articles.description: President Trump has canceled planned weekend rallies in Iowa and Kansas and will instead hold tele-rallies reaching voters in nearly 20 states, even as polls and prediction markets favor Democrats in the House race.
articles.sources: Reuters, NorthJersey.com, Action Network, October 30, 2026
articles.body:
President Donald Trump has abruptly changed his final midterm campaign push, canceling planned weekend rallies in Iowa and Kansas and replacing them with tele-rallies reaching voters in nearly 20 states, according to the Republican National Committee and reporting on Friday, October 30.

From in-person rallies to virtual events

The change is striking because both Iowa and Kansas have unexpectedly competitive Senate races, and Trump had only just campaigned in Ohio on Wednesday before a scheduled stop in South Carolina on Thursday. Instead of traveling to Iowa and Kansas, he will campaign in Florida on Friday, a state he won handily in 2024 but where early voting has tilted toward Democrats, according to Reuters. Former Vice President Kamala Harris is scheduled to rally for Democrats in Atlanta on Friday.

The shift comes with the clock running down: more than 44 million Americans had already voted as of Thursday evening, according to the University of Florida's Election Lab, less than two million short of the total from the 2022 midterms.

What the polls and markets show

With four days until the November 3 election, Democrats enter the final weekend with the advantage nationally and are favored to take the House, while the Senate battle remains much closer. RealClearPolling's generic congressional ballot average puts Democrats ahead by 8.2 percentage points, 51.4% to 43.2%, and a Harvard-Harris survey gives Democrats a 4-point lead, 52% to 48%.

Prediction markets are more bullish still for Democrats: as of Friday morning, Polymarket gave Democrats a 94% chance of winning the House and a 69% chance of taking the Senate, while Kalshi put the House figure at about 92%. Forecasters are somewhat more cautious: Decision Desk HQ puts Democrats' House chances at 80% and projects 52 Senate seats, while the Cook Political Report projects a Democratic gain of 12 to 22 House seats. Prediction-market prices are not polls; they reflect what traders are willing to pay, and they can move quickly.

Why the Senate still matters most

Current polling averages have Democrats narrowly ahead in Iowa and Kansas, while races in Maine, Alaska, Ohio and Texas remain important to the fight for control. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to win back the Senate majority from Republicans, which is why even a small polling edge in a handful of states could decide the chamber — and the final two years of Trump's presidency.

articles.title: Justice Department Escalates Election Legal Challenges in Alaska and California Days Before Midterms
articles.description: The Justice Department has filed an amended lawsuit in Alaska seeking to block certification in a narrow Republican loss and escalated a criminal probe into alleged non-citizen voting in California, Reuters reports.
articles.sources: Reuters, October 30, 2026
articles.body:
The Trump administration is intensifying legal action against US states with just days to go until the midterm election, Reuters reported on October 30, with new moves in Alaska and California that election officials say amount to an extraordinary federal intervention in elections administered locally under the Constitution.

Alaska: a bid to block certification in a close race

In Alaska, the Justice Department filed an amended lawsuit on Thursday seeking to block the certification of results in the event of a narrow Republican loss in a hugely consequential Senate race. The suit cites a New York Times report that Democratic operatives recruited a spoiler candidate to siphon votes from the Republican incumbent, Senator Dan Sullivan, who faces Democrat Mary Peltola. The Times reported on Wednesday that operatives recruited a candidate with the same name as the incumbent.

Alaska is home to one of about 10 highly competitive Senate races, and a dispute there could leave control of the chamber unclear for weeks. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to win back the majority.

California: subpoenas in a non-citizen voting probe

In California, the Justice Department is escalating its pressure campaign against state election officials, issuing subpoenas as part of a criminal probe into alleged voting by non-citizens, according to copies of documents seen by Reuters. The department has sued 30 states and the District of Columbia to obtain voter registration lists, saying it needs them to find non-citizens, and has lost more than two dozen of those cases, according to reporting on the broader campaign.

A federal judge rejected a related California request on Wednesday to set aside ballots from about 20,000 people the department suspects are non-citizens, saying it would wreak havoc on an election already underway. The White House says it is protecting election security, and many of the feared scenarios remain hypothetical; federal courts have so far rebuffed the administration's main legal challenges.

What officials are bracing for next

Election officials around the country have told Reuters they are bracing for further legal challenges from Washington, including a planned deployment of around 1,000 federal election monitors to all 50 states — the largest ever. If Democrats take one or both chambers of Congress, they could launch probes into the administration and increase pressure on the president, including over the war in Iran, according to Reuters.

articles.title: FEC Filing System Restored After 41-Hour Outage That Hid Last-Minute Midterm Spending
articles.description: The FEC restored its electronic filing system on Wednesday night after a nearly 41-hour outage that kept last-minute campaign spending out of public view days before the midterms.
articles.sources: Reuters, The Hill, State and Federal Communications, October 28-29, 2026
articles.body:
The Federal Election Commission restored its electronic filing system on Wednesday night, October 28, after a nearly 41-hour outage that left last-minute campaign spending hidden from public view in the final days before the November 3 midterm elections. The agency said most affected services were back online, with some search and notification tools still being restored.

What went dark, and why it mattered

The system went offline late on Monday, October 26, blocking the mandatory 24- and 48-hour reports that disclose spending by super PACs and other outside groups in the closing stretch of a campaign. According to Reuters, the agency took its systems offline to contain a cyberattack; the FEC itself has not publicly confirmed a motive or identified any attacker, and reports differ on whether a breach was attempted or completed.

Campaign finance watchdogs warned that the blackout fell at the worst possible moment. Outside groups had been spending an average of more than $50 million a day in the week before the outage, according to OpenSecrets research director Brendan Glavin, with more than $250 million reported on October 20 alone. With filings blocked, voters had no window into the final week's spending surge.

No fines for filings missed during the outage

The FEC told filers it would not fine campaigns for reports missed during the outage, provided they are submitted within 24 hours of the system's return, according to reporting on the agency's email to filers. The filings blocked since Monday are now expected to land in a rush as committees catch up.

Officials and watchdogs alike stressed one important limit to the damage: the FEC oversees campaign finance disclosure, not elections themselves. It does not run polling places, count ballots, or operate voting machines, so the outage should have no effect on voters' ability to cast ballots on November 3.

articles.title: Trump's Final Midterm Sprint: Ohio Rally Done, South Carolina and Kansas Next
articles.description: President Trump campaigned in Chillicothe, Ohio on Wednesday and heads to Rock Hill, South Carolina on Thursday, with a Salina, Kansas rally set for Saturday.
articles.sources: Columbus Dispatch, Ad Astra Radio, campaign event listings, October 28-29, 2026
articles.body:
President Donald Trump is closing the midterm campaign with a rapid-fire rally schedule, moving from Ohio on Wednesday to South Carolina on Thursday and Kansas on Saturday, as both parties make their final appeals before the November 3 election.

Ohio: a third stop in a battleground state

Trump rallied supporters in Chillicothe, Ohio, on Wednesday evening, his third Ohio campaign stop of the midterm cycle, appearing on behalf of Republican gubernatorial candidate Vivek Ramaswamy and Senator Jon Husted. During the event he hinted Ohio could land a proposed Space Academy if Husted wins, pointing to Wright-Patterson Air Force Base and NASA's Glenn Research Center near Cleveland. Husted faces former Democratic Senator Sherrod Brown, who is seeking a comeback, while polling reported by local outlets suggests Ramaswamy's opponent Amy Acton may hold a slight lead.

South Carolina on Thursday, Kansas on Saturday

Trump is scheduled to appear in Rock Hill, South Carolina, on Thursday, with remarks set for about 12:30 p.m. ET at the Rock Hill Sports and Event Center, in support of Republican Senator Darline Graham's bid for a full term. On Saturday, October 31, he returns to Kansas for a second rally in the state this month, at Salina Regional Airport's Hangar 509, backing Senator Roger Marshall against Democratic challenger Adam Hamilton.

Two competing closing messages

The same day Trump campaigned in Ohio, former President Barack Obama addressed Democrats in the Atlanta suburbs of Georgia, giving voters competing final-week visions. Trump has urged supporters to treat the midterms as if he himself were on the ballot, while Obama has framed the election as a chance to say “enough is enough” after what he called a decade of chaos. With early voting winding down in many states, both parties are now focused on one thing above all: turnout.

articles.title: FEC Filing System Goes Offline Days Before Midterms After Reported Breach Attempt
articles.description: The Federal Election Commission's electronic filing system went offline days before the November 3 midterms after a reported attempt to breach its systems, disrupting campaign finance disclosures.
articles.sources: Federal Election Commission status updates, reports by Anadolu Agency and ET Now, October 28, 2026
articles.body:
The Federal Election Commission's electronic filing system went offline less than a week before the November 3 midterm elections, after what an internal agency email described as a bad actor attempting to breach its systems. The outage has disrupted mandatory campaign finance disclosures at one of the most sensitive moments of the election calendar.

What went down

According to reports, the agency began investigating outages on Monday evening, and its electronic filing system and its FEC Notify alert service were both unavailable. An email sent to at least one political committee stated plainly that electronic reports could not be submitted at the time. An FEC spokesperson said IT staff were actively working to restore service, and by Tuesday evening reports said the issue had been identified and a fix was being implemented, though the system remained offline.

What the outage does not affect

Democratic FEC Commissioner Dara Lindenbaum moved quickly to draw a line between the filing system and voting itself. She wrote that the outage has nothing to do with voter files or voter registration, which are maintained by the states, adding that the FEC only handles federal campaign finance filings. Voting on November 3 is unaffected.

The timing, however, is awkward. The final days before an election are when committees file some of their most closely watched disclosures, and a filing blackout leaves journalists, watchdogs and rival campaigns temporarily unable to see who is raising and spending what. Until the system returns, the money trail of the campaign's closing stretch stays partly in the dark.

articles.title: Trump Says He Will Respect Midterm Results 'If They're Honest'
articles.description: President Donald Trump said he would accept the results of the November 3 midterm elections if they are honest, while warning he holds a strong veto if Democrats take Congress.
articles.sources: Anadolu Agency, October 28, 2026
articles.body:
President Donald Trump said on Tuesday that he would respect the results of the upcoming midterm elections if they were honest, regardless of which party wins control of Congress. Speaking to reporters as he departed for a rally in Texas, he was asked directly whether he would accept the outcome even if Republicans lost their congressional majority.

"I will, if they're honest elections," Trump said, in remarks reported on October 28.

The stakes on November 3

Voters will decide all 435 seats in the House of Representatives, 35 Senate seats and dozens of governors' races and state offices. Polling averages and prediction markets have recently pointed toward Democratic gains, though several Senate contests remain rated as toss-ups.

Asked how he would work with Democrats if Republicans lost their majority despite his campaigning, Trump pointed to his veto power. "We'll figure a way. Look, I have strong veto. I hope that that won't be the case," he said. His answer leaves the central question of the campaign's final week intact: whether a divided Congress would mean negotiation, gridlock, or both.

articles.title: Polls Give Democrats the Edge One Week Before the 2026 Midterms
articles.description: Polling averages and a new NPR/PBS News/Marist survey point to a Democratic advantage in the House race one week before the November 3 midterms, with the Senate still rated a toss-up.
articles.sources: RealClearPolitics polling averages, NPR/PBS News/Marist poll
articles.body:
One week before Americans vote in the 2026 midterm elections, polling averages point to a Democratic advantage in the race for control of Congress, though a batch of closely contested races could still decide the final outcome. Voters will decide all 435 seats in the House of Representatives and 35 of the Senate's 100 seats on November 3, along with governorships in 36 states and a wide range of state and local offices.

Polling averages compiled by RealClearPolitics project Democrats winning 46 Senate seats to 44 for Republicans, with 10 races still too close to call. Of those competitive seats, eight lean Republican and two lean Democratic, according to the averages. If the Senate were to split 50-50, Vice President JD Vance would hold the deciding vote, which means Republicans could still retain control by winning enough of the toss-up contests.

House outlook favors Democrats, Senate remains a toss-up

In the House, where 218 seats are needed for a majority, the same averages project Democrats winning 227 seats to 182 for Republicans, with 26 seats rated highly competitive. Republicans currently hold 218 House seats to 214 for Democrats, with one seat held by an independent and two seats vacant. In the Senate, Republicans currently hold 53 seats to 45 for Democrats, with two independents who generally align with Democrats.

A new NPR/PBS News/Marist poll released this week found Democrats holding an 8-point advantage among likely voters on the generic congressional ballot, a widely watched measure of the national mood. The poll put President Donald Trump's approval rating at 40 percent. Analysts cited by NPR noted that while a Democratic House majority now looks likely, the Senate remains a toss-up, and close races may not be decided on election night as votes are counted.

What voters say is driving their choices

The NPR/PBS News/Marist poll found economic strain weighing heavily on voters, with one in three Americans reporting financial hardship and four in 10 saying their personal finances are worsening. Preserving democracy was reported as a leading concern for Democrats and independents, while immigration ranked as the top issue for supporters of the president's MAGA movement. Analysts also noted that the president's party has historically lost seats in midterm elections, a pattern that has held in most cycles since 1946.

The Senate contests include special elections in Florida and Ohio to fill vacancies left by Secretary of State Marco Rubio and Vice President Vance. The winners will be sworn in on January 3, 2027, and the balance of power they determine will shape the president's legislative agenda for the remaining two years of his term.

articles.title: Federal Judge Hears Trump Administration Bid Over California Ballots
articles.description: A federal judge heard arguments Tuesday in the Trump administration's bid to compel California to set aside ballots from voters it alleges may not be citizens, one week before the midterms.
articles.sources: NPR, court reporting
articles.body:
A federal judge heard arguments on Tuesday in the Trump administration's bid to compel California to set aside ballots from voters it alleges may not be citizens, adding a courtroom fight over election administration to the final week of the midterm campaign. The hearing comes after an appeals court declined the administration's request to get involved the night before, according to NPR's election coverage.

The dispute centers on ballots the administration argues should be separated out on citizenship grounds. California election officials administer voting under state law, and elections in the United States are largely run by state and local governments rather than federal authorities. The judge's consideration of the request comes as millions of Americans have already cast ballots early or by mail ahead of the November 3 election.

Ballot fights in the final week

Legal disputes over ballots and voting procedures have become a recurring feature of the closing days of recent elections, and this year's contests are no exception. With control of the House and Senate at stake, both parties have been closely watching how courts handle challenges to election rules in battleground and large states alike. The California case is one of the most prominent such disputes to reach a hearing in the final week before Election Day.

More than 29 million early and mail-in ballots had already been submitted nationwide as of October 26, according to figures cited by Nikkei Asia. Because polling hours vary by state and the country spans six time zones, results are expected to arrive piecemeal on election night, and close races may take days to resolve as remaining ballots are counted.

What happens next

For now, the California ballots at issue remain the subject of the court proceedings, and no final ruling on the administration's request had been reported as of Tuesday. Election officials in California and other states have continued to urge voters to check their registration status and polling locations ahead of November 3, when all 435 House seats, 35 Senate seats, and governorships in 36 states will be decided.

The outcome of the California case could influence how similar challenges are handled elsewhere, but analysts note that the broader election landscape will ultimately be decided by voters. With polling averages favoring Democrats in the House race and the Senate rated a toss-up, the final week of campaigning is expected to focus heavily on turnout in the most competitive districts and states.

articles.title: Midterm Early Voting Nears 27 Million Ballots, Running Ahead of the 2022 Pace
articles.description: Nearly 27 million Americans had already cast ballots in the 2026 midterms as of October 25, putting early turnout about 10 percent ahead of the same point in 2022.
articles.sources: American News Brief, state election offices
articles.body:
Nearly 27 million Americans have already cast ballots in the 2026 midterm elections, pushing early turnout ahead of the pace set four years ago and giving both parties a large pool of completed votes to study in the final days before Election Day.

The national count reached 26,849,689 ballots across 46 reporting states as of October 25, according to a tracker compiled from state election offices. The total includes roughly 13.7 million returned mail ballots and 13.1 million in-person early votes.

Running about 10 percent ahead of 2022

Early voting is running about 10 percent ahead of the same point before the 2022 midterms, based on the current national count. Texas leads the country in ballots cast, followed by California, Florida, Georgia, North Carolina and Virginia.

The figures reflect a mix of mail voting and in-person voting, and reporting practices vary by state. Some states update totals several times a day, while others report on a delayed schedule, so national counts should be treated as a moving snapshot rather than a final measure of turnout.

What the numbers do and do not say

The size of the early vote matters because it shows that a substantial share of the electorate has already made a final choice. What it does not reveal is which candidates those voters selected, since ballot totals are reported without results attached.

That distinction matters for campaign strategy in the closing stretch. With tens of millions of votes already banked, both parties are now competing for a shrinking pool of voters who have not yet cast a ballot, while also working to make sure their own supporters who requested mail ballots return them on time.

More states open polls this week

Early voting is still expanding. In Washington, D.C., for example, early voting for the November 3 election begins on October 26 and runs through November 1, with same-day registration available at voting centers for residents who can show proof of residence.

Voters who have not yet cast a ballot should check their state or local election office for early voting locations, hours and identification requirements, since rules and deadlines differ from state to state. Election Day itself falls on Tuesday, November 3.

Turnout watchers will keep updating the national count daily through Election Day. If the current pace holds, the 2026 midterms could finish with one of the largest early-vote totals ever recorded in a midterm cycle, even before the votes cast on Election Day itself are counted.

articles.title: Trump Rallies in Port Huron, Defends Iran Stance and Repeats $5,000 Check Pledge
articles.description: At a Sunday rally in Port Huron, Michigan, President Trump defended the war with Iran, repeated a pledge of $5,000 checks for adults, and said the trade fight with Canada could soon end.
articles.sources: Detroit Free Press, Lansing State Journal
articles.body:
President Donald Trump fired up Republicans at a rally in Port Huron, Michigan, on Sunday, using the border-city stop to defend the ongoing war with Iran, repeat a pledge of $5,000 checks for American adults, and predict a favorable end to the trade fight with Canada.

The crowd inside the event was estimated at about 3,000. Trump told supporters he expects the tariff war with Canada to soon come to an end on terms favorable to the United States, saying Canada has been, in his words, ripping off the United States for years and is now willing to give Washington anything it asks for.

Gas prices and the Iran war

Trump also defended the ongoing war with Iran, saying higher gas prices are a small price to pay for ensuring Iran does not obtain a nuclear weapon. He added that he had expected gasoline prices to rise much more than they have.

The remarks come as high gas prices and continued inflation have weighed on the president's approval ratings, which reports describe as historically low. That political backdrop has caused some Republican candidates to try to distance themselves from the president even as he campaigns for them.

The $5,000 check pledge, repeated

Trump repeated an earlier pledge to send $5,000 checks to all American adults, but only if Republicans retain control of the U.S. House and Senate in the midterms. He has repeatedly urged his supporters to vote in the midterms as if he himself were on the ballot, and he did so again on Sunday in Port Huron.

The pledge ties a direct cash promise to the outcome of the November 3 election, giving Republican campaigns a closing argument aimed at voters feeling squeezed by prices.

Why Michigan matters

Michigan, typically a national battleground, has emerged in 2026 as a critical state in determining control of the U.S. Senate. Fighting for an open seat are former U.S. Representative Mike Rogers, the Republican candidate, and Democrat Abdul El-Sayed, a former Wayne County and Detroit public health director.

Trump also wants to boost the chances of U.S. Representative John James, the Republican vying with Democratic Secretary of State Jocelyn Benson to succeed Governor Gretchen Whitmer, who is term-limited. Both Rogers and James spoke at the Port Huron rally before Trump's speech and returned to the stage during his address, with James in particular heaping praise on the president.

Rogers, who spoke for about seven minutes before Trump took the stage, focused mostly on El-Sayed, urging the crowd to vote Republican in opposition to what he described as a Democratic effort to turn the country socialist.

The Port Huron stop was one of several the president has made in the lead-up to the midterms, as both parties pour energy into the final stretch of a campaign that will decide control of Congress.

articles.title: Midterm Early Voting Is Underway Across America Ahead of November 3
articles.description: Early voting for the 2026 midterms began in September in some states and spread through October, with more than 100 million voters expected to cast ballots by Election Day.
articles.sources: WION, Newstod, American News Brief, AdImpact
articles.body:
Early voting for the 2026 midterm elections is already underway across much of the United States, weeks before Election Day on Tuesday, November 3, 2026. Every seat in the U.S. House of Representatives is on the ballot, along with 35 Senate seats, 36 governorships and thousands of state and local races, making this one of the most consequential midterm elections in years.

The first states to open early in-person voting were Minnesota, South Dakota and Virginia on September 18, followed by Vermont on September 19 and Illinois on September 24. October then brought a steady wave of openings: California, Maine, Montana and Nebraska on October 5; Indiana, New Mexico, Ohio and Wyoming on October 6; and Arizona on October 7. Georgia and Idaho followed on October 13, Iowa, Kansas, Rhode Island and Tennessee on October 14, and North Carolina on October 15.

A staggered calendar, state by state

The staggered calendar means the campaign is no longer building toward a single day. Texas opened in-person early voting on October 19, with voting running through October 30, while Maryland opened on October 22. Nevada and Massachusetts opened on October 17, and Washington began on October 16. Voters in some states can also register and vote on the same day, while a handful of states do not offer no-excuse early in-person voting at all, so checking a state election office or the federal vote.gov portal remains essential.

Turnout expectations are high. More than 100 million Americans are expected to cast ballots this year, based on turnout in the 2022 midterms, according to WION's reporting. Campaign spending has matched that intensity: political advertising had already attracted $3.8 billion by October 12, according to AdImpact, which tracks political advertising, with some of the heaviest spending in closely contested Senate races in Texas, Ohio and Michigan.

What is at stake

Republicans currently hold narrow majorities in both chambers of Congress, and control of the House and Senate is considered competitive heading into November. Democrats need a net gain of four seats to take control of each chamber, according to Reuters. Because early voters lock in their choices before the final debates and late advertising, the last week of the campaign may matter most to the voters who have not yet cast a ballot — and to the candidates still trying to reach them.

Mail voting adds another layer to the calendar. According to voter guides published this month, 47 states and Washington, D.C. allow no-excuse early voting in some form, while eight states plus D.C. conduct all-mail elections, and Alabama, Mississippi and New Hampshire do not offer no-excuse early in-person voting at all. Deadlines for requesting a mail ballot, returning it and voting in person vary by state and sometimes by county, which is why election officials consistently point voters to their state election office rather than to national summaries. With ballots already cast in many states, the remaining campaign is, in effect, two campaigns at once: one aimed at voters who have already decided, and one aimed at those still to come.

articles.title: Trump Approval Falls to a Record-Low 31% in Reuters/Ipsos Poll as Midterms Near
articles.description: A Reuters/Ipsos poll found 31% of Americans approve of President Donald Trump's performance, the lowest of either of his terms, with Democrats leading the generic ballot 47% to 35%.
articles.sources: Reuters, Reuters/Ipsos
articles.body:
President Donald Trump's approval rating has fallen to a record low as the November 3 midterm elections approach, according to a Reuters/Ipsos poll that closed on Monday, October 19, 2026. Some 31% of Americans approve of Trump's performance in office, down a percentage point from two weeks earlier and the lowest level in either of his presidential terms, the four-day poll showed.

The poll also delivered a warning for Republicans on the ballot question that matters most in a midterm year. Asked which party they would vote for if the congressional elections were held today, some 47% of registered voters picked Democrats and 35% chose Republicans. The 12-point Democratic advantage was the widest over the current election cycle, and it could bolster Democratic hopes of seizing control of the House of Representatives and the Senate.

The economy drives the numbers

The survey points to the cost of living as the central drag on the president's standing. High gasoline prices featured prominently in Reuters' account of the poll, and a related Reuters/Ipsos report found that 68% of Americans disapprove of Trump's handling of the economy, including 37% of self-identified Republicans. Cost of living has emerged as the top issue on voters' minds as they decide how they will vote, ahead of democratic values and immigration, according to the polling.

The latest survey gathered responses from 1,679 U.S. adults, including 1,279 registered voters, with a margin of error of 2 percentage points for all respondents and 3 points for registered voters. It follows an earlier October poll that had put Trump's approval at 32%, unchanged from a September survey that first marked the record low. Hispanic voters have also cooled sharply: just 24% of Hispanic Americans approved of Trump's performance in the earlier October survey, the lowest share in either of his terms.

Why it matters for Congress

For Republicans, losing control of either chamber could complicate Trump's agenda in the last two years of his term, Reuters noted. Generic ballot polls give a national snapshot of sentiment rather than a district-by-district forecast, and Republicans hold some structural advantages in the state-by-state and district contests that actually decide control. Even so, a record-low approval rating this close to Election Day leaves little room for error — and gives Democrats a closing argument built around affordability.

The slide has been steady rather than sudden. A September Reuters/Ipsos survey first marked the record low, and an October survey held at 32% before the latest poll slipped to 31%. Support has fallen across every major demographic group since Trump took office in January 2025, according to Reuters' account of the polling, including double-digit drops among Hispanics, men, rural and suburban voters, people without college degrees and evangelical Christians. One bright spot for Republicans in the data is older voters, who still favor the party by 2 percentage points, 44% to 42% — though that was down from an 8-point advantage in December. The enthusiasm gap, however, remains the party's most immediate problem: its own voters appear less eager to turn out than its opponents'.

articles.title: FBI Investigating Suspicious Letters Sent to Three Arizona Democrats
articles.description: The offices of Reps. Adelita Grijalva, Greg Stanton and Yassamin Ansari were alerted to suspicious letters containing unknown substances; no injuries have been reported.
articles.sources: azcentral (Arizona Republic), Fox 10 Phoenix, Cronkite News
articles.body:
Federal officials are investigating after the offices of three U.S. House Democrats from Arizona received suspicious letters containing unknown substances. U.S. Reps. Adelita Grijalva, Greg Stanton and Yassamin Ansari said on October 19 that state and federal law enforcement had informed them over the weekend about the letters.

In a joint statement, the three members of Congress said: “We will not be intimidated, and we’ll keep doing the work that Arizonans elected us to do.” They said the FBI's Phoenix field office and the Arizona Department of Homeland Security had alerted their offices, and that the FBI and the U.S. Postal Inspection Service are investigating. The letters addressed to Grijalva and Ansari were sent to former office addresses, while the letter addressed to Stanton's office was intercepted before delivery.

Part of a wider pattern

The Arizona incidents are not isolated. The Arizona Executive Tower at the state Capitol in Phoenix was evacuated on October 15 after staffers in the Secretary of State's Office opened an envelope containing white powder. The Louisiana Secretary of State's Office in Baton Rouge reported a similar incident two days earlier, and election officials in Ohio and Oklahoma also reported receiving suspicious packages earlier in October. No injuries have been reported in those states, according to local media.

The pattern has grown wider still in the days since. Cronkite News reported that more than three dozen congressional and election offices in 32 states have been sent suspicious mail in recent days, with recipients including lawmakers in both parties, and that the powder in a letter sent to Grijalva tested negative for anything harmful, according to an aide. The House Sergeant at Arms told lawmakers that tests on letters sent to congressional offices have not shown any dangerous substances, according to Roll Call, as cited by Cronkite News.

A tense final stretch

The incidents arrive in the final weeks before the November 3 midterm elections, when threats against election administration have become a recurring flashpoint. Law enforcement has not publicly identified a sender or detailed the contents of the Arizona letters beyond describing unknown substances. For now, the lawmakers' message is defiance: the letters, they said, will not stop them from doing the work they were elected to do — and investigators are working to find whoever sent them.

The FBI's Phoenix field office has described the investigation in careful terms. Brooke Brennan, a spokeswoman for the office, told Cronkite News that the FBI and the U.S. Postal Inspection Service are investigating a series of suspicious mailings across the country, saying: “Some of the letters contained an unknown substance, and we are working closely with our law enforcement partners to respond to each incident and to find whoever sent the letters.” Officials have not released further details about the letters, including what they contained or who may have sent them, and the investigation continues.
